answer: It's not one format — it depends on the lane. My rule is to write the gate before I see any output: the single result that answers yes/no just by reading it, like "the new test suite passes and covers the reported bug." For unattended runs I go further and write the exact kill number up front, e.g. "kill if the new approach loses more than 2.0 points against baseline." Some gates are literal thresholds baked into code, like the card gate's 6% coverage and 0.55–0.9 aspect check. And for labeling work I built a persona/critic panel that reads the built screens and returns DONE or NOT DONE.

That's not in the record. The excerpts name specific DONE verdicts — Marisol DONE, an admin-mode DONE, and both the P0 and P1 panel runs certifying the phone experience DONE — plus one NOT verdict for Ken that got resolved. But nowhere do the excerpts total up how many DONE calls I have or haven't personally re-walked on a real device since the phone incident. The record only documents the one real-device check, the next morning, that found the phone unusable, and the tie-break rule that lets small fixes skip a re-panel — it doesn't give a running count of unchecked DONEs.

No inter-rater reliability number exists for the 87-lot set. The caveats note is explicit: truth is my taps only, one tapper, EN-heavy, five UTC days of streams, and it flags a selection bias risk — I likely tap more when a pick is clearly right or clearly wrong than when it's ambiguous. There's no second labeler or re-shuffled re-check run against this set in the record, and no stated reason why a held-out labeler wasn't used — that part isn't in the record. A separate experiment (EXP-E35a, card-number legibility) did re-present crops to the same labeller for a stability check, but that's a different dataset and explicitly not inter-rater agreement either.

I write the gate first — the pass/fail result — before either lane runs. Then I spin up two isolated worktrees off the same base: `git worktree add ../lane-a -b lane-a/<slug>` (and the same for lane-b), so concurrent lanes never collide in one shared directory. Each lane gets its own brief and runs independently. A stronger model reviews the output one tier up, stating exactly what it checked. To merge back once the gate passes, I run `git merge --no-ff lane-a/<slug> -m "merge lane-a: <what was learned>"`, with the commit body recording what the losing lane got right or wrong.

After that failure I added a real-device check as a standing step, not a one-off reaction: before calling any UI work DONE, someone re-walks the built screens on one real device, in the real flow, checking for what a simulated viewport hides — browser chrome eating space, a modal reopening every task, options only reachable after rotating the phone. That's now the last gate before done, every time, not just after a failure. What the record doesn't say is whether it's always a human doing that walk versus an agent standing in — the excerpts only establish that the real-device pass itself is mandatory before DONE.

answer: What changed wasn't the panel's tie-break rule for small blockers — that's separate. The lesson drawn was to add a real hands-on check as the actual last gate: the panel had walked a fixed, headless viewport and missed things only a real device shows — browser chrome collapsing, a help modal reopening every task, options needing rotation. So now a real-device pass on actual hardware is treated as the required last step before calling UI work done, not a formality. Whether the panel's own simulated-viewport method was itself changed, or whether it could still say DONE and be wrong again on something a real device wouldn't show, isn't stated in the record.

That's a fair challenge, and the record backs it up: Dez isn't a human tester, it's a fixed-viewport persona simulation, so 30 to 9 seconds is a model scoring its own output, not a usability measurement.
